description.value: The study investigated whether expected monetary and erotic reward values are represented on a common neural currency in the human ventral striatum during an incentive delay task without explicit choice.

spans.text: The present study investigated the use of a common neural currency for representing expected reward value in the absence of choice.

model_settings.value: First-level fMRI responses were modeled in a general linear model with separate regressors for monetary and erotic anticipation cues, reward outcomes, non-rewarded outcomes, and control scrambled pictures. Anticipation cues were modeled as 2.5-second box-car functions; outcome responses were modeled as events and regressors were convolved with the canonical hemodynamic response function. Reward probability and intensity were included as orthogonal parametric regressors for anticipation. Probability and hedonic-rating covariates were included for outcome conditions, and six motion parameters were nuisance regressors. A 128-second high-pass filter was applied. Group-level analyses used second-level contrasts and cluster-level P < 0.05 whole-brain correction with voxel-level uncorrected P < 0.001 or less.

description.value: Participants viewed an erotic cue predicting an erotic image with 25%, 50%, or 75% probability and low or high intensity, then completed the target discrimination task within 1 second to obtain the opportunity to view the erotic outcome. Low-intensity images showed females in underwear or bathing suits; high-intensity images showed naked females in an inviting posture.

spans.text: Nudity being the main criteria driving the reward value of erotic stimuli, we separated them into a ‘low intensity’ group displaying females in underwear or bathing suits and a ‘high intensity’ group displaying naked females in an inviting posture.

If they answered correctly within <1 s, they were then allowed to view the outcome of the pseudorandom draw.

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to perform a target discrimination task after the anticipatory cue and delay. They had to identify a triangle or square by pressing the corresponding button within 1 second; successful performance allowed them to view the outcome of the pseudorandom draw. After rewarded outcomes, they rated how pleased they were on a continuous 1–9 scale.

spans.text: Following a delay period, participants had to perform a target discrimination task within <1 s.

stimuli.value: The task presented monetary and erotic incentive cues indicating reward type, probability, and intensity. Monetary rewards were low amounts of €1, €2, or €3 or high amounts of €10, €11, or €12. Erotic rewards were low-intensity images of females in underwear or bathing suits and high-intensity images of naked females in an inviting posture. Non-rewarded and control trials presented scrambled versions of the reward images. A question mark served as the delay stimulus, and triangles and squares served as discrimination targets.

spans.text: A similar element of surprise was introduced for the monetary rewards by randomly varying the amounts at stake: the low amounts were either 1, 2 or 3 € and the high amounts were either 10, 11 or 12 €.
